Abstract 23

REBCO-based superconducting magnets are considered crucial to the long-awaited realization of 24 commercially viable controlled thermonuclear fusion via compact reactor architectures. To expand the 25 current understanding of how the inherently reduced shielding of these proposed designs affects the 26 radiation-sensitive high temperature superconductors, the activation spectra and microstructure of 27 REBCO tapes irradiated more traditionally with fission-reactor neutrons were compared to those 28 irradiated with the higher-fidelity fusion-like spectrum produced by thick target deuteron breakup in a 29 first-of-its-kind irradiation experiment on these coated conductors. For the fusion-like case, several peaks 30 in the activation spectrum confirmed high-threshold nuclear reactions, and SEM revealed superficial 31 alterations to the most intensely irradiated area. TEM revealed that although both sets of microstructures 32 appeared strained, the 14 MeV-irradiated damage manifested as milder patches of subcascades and large 33 voids, with no large amorphous clusters classically associated with REBCO fission irradiations, as 34 confirmed by our own fission samples. Computational analysis on the visually indistinguishable respective 35 lattice strains revealed comparable damage metrics of the fusion-like samples to fission samples, despite 36 the much lower total fluences on the former. The nuclear physics origins of these findings and their 37 implications for the superconducting properties are also discussed. These results present an important 38 preliminary step in the rigorous technical readiness qualifications required by this pivotal technology in 39 the burgeoning REBCO-based compact fusion industry. 40

Introduction 41

Fusion, a promising, but so-far commercially unachieved source of clean energy [1], may be realized in 42

the near future by utilizing Rare-Earth Barium Copper Oxide (REBCO) coated conductors as the high- 43

temperature superconducting (HTS) magnets in tested and proven reactor architectures like the tokamak 44

or stellarator [2], [3]. These compact designs are aimed at being smaller, and therefore quicker to build 45

and more cost effective than the world’s leading fusion project, the International Thermonuclear 46

Experimental Reactor (ITER), whose toroidal field coils are based on more traditional low-temperature 47

superconductors (LTS) to confine the plasma during operation [4]. A major consequence of compact 48

designs is the increased radiation exposure from the plasma on the surrounding materials due to the 49

reduced room for shielding. The intense radiation may have a particularly disabling effect on the toroidal 50

field (TF) magnets [5], among other components. These effects include displacement damage, activation, 51

transmutation, gas production, swelling, embrittlement, and irradiation-induced creep [6], [7]. Besides 52

compromising mechanical properties, these can also affect the superconductor performance by altering 53

the pinning landscape and therefore vortex dynamics of REBCO [8]. 54

Interestingly, the change in the key superconducting parameter of critical current (Jc) has been shown 55

to undergo a complex variation, rather than a trivial monotonic decrease that one would imply from first 56

principles [9]. Studies attempting to replicate the effects of fusion reactor conditions on REBCO do show 57

that irradiation results in the formation of additional irradiation-induced artificial pinning centers (APCs) 58

[10]. This change in microstructure appears to have two competing effects on the overall Jc in these type- 59

II superconductors: an initial, ostensibly parabolic increase from enhanced vortex pinning until some 60

critical point of defect-density saturation, and a simultaneous linear decrease due to copper oxide plane 61

and chain damage [11]. Since the former is proportionally greater than the latter, at first the new APCs 62

benefit the net Jc, but eventually, as this benefit attenuates, the overall critical current begins to trend 63

downward and is suppressed altogether at some critical fluence. Understanding the rate and nature of 64

this variation and ultimate degradation is therefore crucial for the eventual implementation and 65

commercial success of REBCO-based compact fusion plants. 66

While some irradiation studies have been performed on REBCO, they have mostly relied on ions Error! 67 Reference source not found., [13], or fission reactor neutrons [14], [15] that have generally softer neutron 68

spectra when compared to what can be expected at the magnet location for compact fusion reactors [5]. 69

This study aimed to expand upon the known materials-focused literature by conducting thick target 70

deuteron breakup (TTDB) neutron irradiations, which can deliver the harder, 14-MeV-dominated, fusion- 71

like spectrum we anticipate in-service. We began by following up on a study by coauthor Iio et al. [16], 72

examining their ‘used’ fission-irradiated and transport-measured samples, now through the lens of 73

materials science. Following previously unreported TTDB irradiations on these modern coated conductors, 74

we compared the fission samples with the fusion-like neutron-irradiated ones using radionuclide analysis, 75

scanning and transmission electron microscopy, and computational analysis. 76

Neutron Activation Analysis confirms high-threshold inelastic reactions 79

The activation gamma spectra for both SuperPower and Fujikura BR2 samples are shown in Fig. 1a, and 80 Fig. 1b, respectively, both exhibiting several prominent peaks. As detailed in the methods section, the 81 samples are labeled by their make (SCS for SuperPower, FYSC for Fujikura), method of irradiation (BR2 for 82 Belgian Reactor 2/fission neutrons, 88-Inch for 88-Inch Cyclotron/fusion-like neutrons), and dose (‘P’ for 83

pristine/unirradiated, ‘LD’ for the lower fission dose of 8.23×1021 n/m2, ‘HD’ for the higher fission dose 84

7.92×1022 n/m2, ‘C1’ for the lower fusion-like dose 6×1016 n/m2, and ‘C2’ for the higher fusion-like dose 85

6×1017 n/m2). Also note that BR2 samples where assayed 3 years after irradiation, while the 88-Inch 86 samples were done within hours of irradiation. For BR2 samples, the peak positions between SuperPower 87 and Fujikura spectra differ by less than 1 keV in most cases, which falls within the expected energy 88 resolution limits of standard gamma detectors. The activation gamma spectrum for an SCS-88-Inch-C1 89 sample positioned between 14° and 68° of the central 14 MeV cone (see methods) is shown in Fig. 1c and 90 Fig. 1d, also with prominent peaks identified and labeled. 91

For the BR2 gamma spectra, the most intense peaks were observed at 1174 keV and 1332 keV, 92 corresponding to the decay of cobalt-60 (⁶⁰Co), which is produced via reactions such as neutron capture 93 on nickel ⁵⁹Ni(n,γ)⁶⁰Ni followed by β⁻ decay, and 63Cu(n,α)⁶⁰Co, with zero-threshold 59Co(n,γ) radiative 94 capture contributing via moderated neutrons later in the cascade. This is expected given the high nickel 95 content in the Hastelloy substrate. The ⁶⁰Co peaks for the Fujikura samples were relatively higher 96 compared to the SuperPower samples, possibly due to the substrate thickness of the former being 50% 97 greater than that of the latter. In fact, if we account for the copper, the FYSC-SCH04 tapes are ~20% 98 thicker than the SCS-4050AP tapes, corroborated well by the ~25% higher activity of the Fujikura 99 samples, as reported in Table 1. Though the ⁶⁰Co peaks are indicative of reaction thresholds around 1– 100 2 MeV expected of fission spectra, we also see a 137Cs peak, indicative of high-threshold reactions such as 101 the 137Ba(n,p)137Cs channel which opens up ~7–8 MeV. The 137Cs peak persists relative to the ⁶⁰Co peak 102 due to the former’s longer half-life of 30.05 y compared to 5.27 y of the latter. Collectively, these results 103 support the conclusion that both thermal and fast neutron-induced reactions contributed to the observed 104 activation products. This reflects the characteristic mixed neutron energy spectrum of the BR2 reactor, 105 typical of fission sources, with two dominant components: a thermal peak below 0.1 eV and a fast peak 106 around ~1–2 MeV. 107

For the 88-Inch REBCO samples irradiated with a 14-MeV-peaked spectrum, however, an evidently 108 different activation profile is observed. The resulting gamma spectrum shows a prominent shift in both 109 the radionuclides produced and the scaled relative peak intensities, compared to the BR2’s fission- 110 spectrum activation. Notably, high-threshold reactions such as 138Ba(n,np)137Cs, 63Cu(n,α)60Co, and 111

62Ni(n,α)59Fe dominate, consistent with the hard neutron energy distribution favoring (n,2n) and (n,α) 112 channels. Strong features such as the 88Y lines at 898 and 1835 keV underscore this energy dependence, 113 as well as highlight the capacity of this Rare-Earth for neutron multiplication. The latter is striking since it 114 means that the yttrium, which sits at the heart of the necessarily highly-ordered modified-perovskite 115 superconductor unit cell, has the ability to release neutrons energetic enough to result in cascades of their 116 own. Though any initial 88Y signature in the BR2 samples would have decayed beyond detectability due to 117 the 106.6-day half-life, the same could not be said about the 137Cs signature, since its 30-year half-life 118 would have resulted in a peak which persisted by the time the measurement was made. In fact, despite 119 the relative scarcity of neutrons energetic enough to overcome this threshold, the signature is prominent 120 in the BR2 samples because the substantially larger total irradiation fluence compensates for this. In other 121 words, the 137Cs peak in the BR2 samples are due to the larger fluence and long half-life, whereas in the 122 88-Inch samples it is due to the harder neutron spectrum. The 138Ba(n,np)137Cs reaction is well-known to 123 have a high energetic threshold ~11.23 MeV, and is an example of a true disparity between the effects 124 of the fission and fusion-like spectra. Overall, these benchmark nuclear data experiments are crucial for 125 enabling high-fidelity Monte Carlo simulations of these superconductors for compact fusion reactor 126 engineers worldwide. 127

SEM shows thermomechanical degradation of REBCO tapes under direct beam irradiation 134

*Figure 2 shows side-by-side SEM of the exposed REBCO layers of pristine and neutron-irradiated 135*

samples. Aside from the central beam-spot irradiated area (discussed below), etched surfaces essentially 136

looked indistinguishable from their pristine counterparts, all matching the classic SEM of REBCO coated- 137

conductors in literature [17]–[19]. As exemplified by the pristine sample in Fig. 2a, typical SEM 138

micrographs (ab-plane coincident with image plane, c-axis out of page/screen) show the highly-textured 139

REBCO pseudo-single-crystal (dark background) populated by a few classic defects: usually porosity, Cu-O 140

or Ba-Cu-O grains (light circular precipitates), and so-called a-axis grains (square/rectangular objects), 141

which are still REBCO grains—though highly misoriented—where the a-axis of unit cell aligns normal to 142 the ab-planar surface instead of the c-axis. The defects present—as well as their size, density, and spatial 143 distribution—depend on parameters such as the thickness to which the REBCO layer is grown and the 144 dopant mol % used to form the APCs (which as mentioned enhance vortex pinning/critical current), and 145 typically vary extensively. Even for the highest-dose samples of each irradiation type shown in Figs. 4b– 146 4d, all defects and their relative densities appeared typical for REBCO. 147

However, the 88-Inch samples positioned near/coincident with the beam spot ∼0° were uniquely 148

affected, resulting in a few key superficial alterations. In Fig. 2e, we see an SEM image of the exposed 149

REBCO layer in the region directly impacted by the beam, including its less-affected borders. The region 150

within the white dashed lines outline the most intensely affected area, which exhibited altered relief and 151

compromised electrical conductivity, as evidenced by the charging visible. Along the boundary, other 152

distinct features are observed, including swelling (Fig. 2f) and a polygonal cellular surface pattern (Fig. 2g). 153

The unique microstructural changes observed in the beam-spot-aligned sample could be relevant to 154

REBCO positioned directly in-line with the diverter of a compact tokamak, which is expected to see 155

substantially higher fluxes relative to other segments along the TF D-coil [5], and is worth some brief 156 discourse. As shown in the higher magnification SEM in Fig. 2h, the polygonal pattern superficially 157

resembles grains, but it is unlikely to reflect the underlying REBCO texture, as the true grains in epitaxial 158

REBCO films are sub-micrometer in scale. Instead, the observed cellular relief is consistent with the 159

intrinsic MOCVD colony morphology of the REBCO thin film. It may be postulated that local overheating 160

during irradiation thermally induced surface etching, thereby enhancing the surface relief—via vacancy- 161

driven grooving and minor oxygen loss—ultimately sharpening the apparent cellular patterns that 162

represent the coalesced growth islands containing the true columnar grains of REBCO. 163

These columns are readily visible as variations in contrast across the length of the REBCO cross-sections 175

(discussed below), and are sub-micron in size and thus much smaller than the cellular pattern’s islands. 176

Similar patterns for thermally etched ceramics like Yttria-Stabilized Zirconia (YSZ) are also noted in 177

literature [20]. This interpretation was further supported by the absence of comparable cellular contrast 178

in unheated control regions, and EDS additionally precluded the possibility that the material was anything 179

other than Rare-earth Barium Copper Oxide. 180

As for the result on the relief of the thin film, several theories were discussed, including irradiation- 181

induced transmutation blistering and eutectic/liquid-metal attack with subsequent cavitation and cap 182

rupture. Given the irradiation conditions—10 µC of 40 MeV deuterons fully stopped in a 7 mm Be breakup 183

target in direct contact with the REBCO tape over a 60 second exposure—the observed surface features 184

cannot be attributed to hydrogen or helium blistering, as the neutron fluence of ~10¹⁶ nm⁻² and implanted 185

deuteron dose are several orders of magnitude below known blistering thresholds in ceramics [21]. The 186

idea of eutectic or liquid-metal attack was entertained but ultimately discarded too since Ag–Ni/Hastelloy 187

systems lack a low-temperature eutectic and the calculated beam heating is insufficient to reach the 188

melting point of Ag. Instead, simple thermal modeling shows that localized beam energy deposition could 189

raise the beryllium and adjacent REBCO/silver stack by several hundred degrees Celsius. Such transient 190

overheating is sufficient to induce Ag thinning and partial dewetting, REBCO oxygen loss, and interfacial 191

delamination, consistent with the dark streaks and rumpled morphology observed upon visual inspection. 192

The damage is therefore best explained as thermomechanical degradation driven by transient beam 193

heating, not irradiation-induced gas blistering or eutectic interaction. 194

Discussion 8

We begin with the more traditional BR2 fission-neutron-irradiated samples. Here, we restate what 9

Linden et al. pointed out in their forerunning work [10]: “from the study of 100s of these images, [they] 10 found no systematic differences between the typical periodic lattice structure of irradiated and 11 unirradiated samples”; a statement which we resoundingly confirmed. So few cascade-induced large 12 amorphous clusters were seen that even a statistical analysis of their distribution could not be made. From 13 first principles, and factoring in the geometry of a standard REBCO coated conductor cross-section, if we 14 assume that all fast (typically > 0.1 MeV) neutrons result in cascade amorphization ~10 nm in diameter, 15 the high-dose irradiation would result in ~160% reduction in the superconductor area. Based on the fact 16 that for similar fluences, Unterrainer et al. previously reported not just nonzero Jc, but improved Jc [9], we 17

may conclude that it truly is only the fastest neutrons that may result in sizable and thermally persistent 18

amorphous clusters. If for example we instead only looked at the portion of the ~1022 m-2 fluence in 19 Unterrainer’s case with energies > 10 MeV then the fraction of cross-section amorphization becomes 20

~2%, which is much closer to the estimates based on direct TEM observations discussed by this study, 21

Linden et al., and the pioneering work done in the early 1990s by Frischherz et al. [22]. In other words, 22 the generation of relatively few isolated cascades in an otherwise apparently intact (though strained) 23 matrix cannot explain the superconductivity degradation seen by Unterrainer’s and Iio’s previous 24 superconductivity tests on neutron irradiation REBCO. Even if we account for as-fabricated APCs, which 25 in modern coated conductors may occupy 3 −4% of the cross-sectional area [23], it is still abundantly 26 clear that reduction of the effective supercurrent-carrying area by large (TEM-visible) amorphous clusters 27 is not the primary reason for Jc suppression at critical fluences. 28

As Linden points out, the suppression of superconductivity may be explained by smaller defects such 29 as clusters of vacancies or interstitials that, while largely undetectable by traditional TEM, could permeate 30 the REBCO layer. It may be postulated that the distortions seen in Fig. 5b are an example of such a class 31 of pervasive defect, though more visible here than in Linden’s work due to the differences between the 32 BR2’s spectrum (our samples) and the TRIGA MARK II’s (Linden’s/Unterrainer’s groups’ samples). 33


<!-- Page 19 -->


Compared to the BR2 reactor, which provides a high neutron flux with a substantial fast and epithermal 34 component, the TRIGA MARK II operates at significantly lower power and produces a much softer, 35 predominantly thermal neutron spectrum. As a result, one may expect that the BR2 has a greater capacity 36 to form larger defects than the TRIGA MARK II. Along this line of reasoning, the smeared lattice distortions 37 are likely the superposition of many nanoscale cascade cores (or mini-cascades)—precisely what Linden 38 proposed for the almost identically looking defects he saw in his ion irradiations (compare Fig. 5b with 39 Figure 4.9 of [24]). The higher fast-neutron component may also explain why, on average, our large 40 clusters were bigger than those reported by Linden. This disparity challenges the traditional binary 41 classification of neutron energies as “thermal” or “fast”—a convention heavily relied upon within the 42 literature of this subfield—since it seems even between fission reactors, differences in the fast/epithermal 43 content produce measurable microstructural changes. Moreover, because the fast component of a fission 44 reactor's neutron flux drops off precipitously above ~1 MeV, studies in the literature often overlook the 45 high-threshold inelastic reactions that would be significant in compact fusion reactors. By contrast, the 46

spectrum projected at the magnet location in such devices spans 1 to 14 MeV—precisely the energy range 47 where these inelastic channels open, become competitive with, and even dominate the elastic 48 contribution to scattering. 49

This brings us to the novel 88-Inch Cyclotron-irradiated samples. Firstly, it is unexpected that— 50

regardless of lamella, subsample, or fluence—no large amorphous clusters indicative of catastrophic 51

cascade events were found. Using the same assumptions as before, and the known nuclear cross sections 52

of the elements in this HTS, one may estimate around 8 × 108 scattering events over the course of the 53

irradiation. This would translate to about a ~0.13 cascades per square μm, with amorphous cluster sizes 54

even larger than those observed in the high-dose BR2 samples due to the harder neutron spectrum. This 55

was not seen. In fact, it was this apparent lack of any large localized amorphous irradiation features that 56

was most striking about the 88-Inch sample survey, with only relatively mild patches of contrast 57

modulation scattered across the lattice observed. The void phenomenon was, however, remarkable, 58

especially since there was no simple or obvious explanation for its existence. One may naively attribute 59

them to gas production, but the transmutation yields on the constituent atoms are orders of magnitude 60

too small given the maximum irradiation fluence.  To fully grasp our rationale as to why only the 14 MeV- 61

neutron-irradiated lamellae exhibited this, as well as more quantitatively analyze the more subtle 62

irradiation features gathered by TEM, we briefly review some fundamental nuclear physics and how their 63

implications on the microstructure may be garnered by computational techniques. 64

Two aspects of nuclear physics that emerge at very fast energies (~14 MeV) which affect radiation 65 damage estimates may help explain the differences in the observed microstructural damage [7]: reduced 66 elastic scattering contribution and supplanting inelastic contribution to damage cross section. First, recall 67

that in modified Kinchin-Pease theory, the angularly-dependent dpa cross section is given by: 68

forward peaked—an entirely wavelike property common to all medium-to-heavy nuclides at these 76 neutron energies—the vast majority of scatters occur at very low angles. When this large peak for the 77 differential cross section at ߠ= 0 is weighted into the (1 −cosߠ) factor of Eq. 1, the net result is a 78 suppressed elastic contribution to the damage cross section. So, somewhat counterintuitively, raising to 79 very fast neutron energies result in diminishing contributions to classic “pool ball” Kinchin-Pease type 80 elastic collision cascades. 81

Secondly, the practical consequence of irradiating with 14 MeV neutrons is that non-elastic channels 82

carry a comparatively larger share of the damage production. The predominant inelastic reactions 83

anticipated—(n,n') on medium/heavy constituents producing 10–13 MeV secondaries, and (n,2n)/(n,np) 84

on Cu/Ba/RE producing 1-3 MeV secondaries—shift the momentum since some of the incoming neutron’s 85 kinetic energy is used to excite the target nuclei. The relatively reduced outgoing kinetic energy of the 86 inelastically scattered neutron imparts significant recoil energy to the Primary Knock-on Atom (PKA) even 87 for glancing angles, as required by the conservation of momentum. This effect is amplified further for 88 multi-particle emission channels where the inelastic vector sums against two ejectiles, routinely producing 89

tens-of-keV PKAs. Moreover, these inelastic reactions are less forward-peaked so large-angle events are 90

more probable, which, when incorporated into equation 1, result in larger displacement cross sections. 91

The net result of these effects is the substantial increase in average PKA energies. Overall, increasing 92

neutron energies to 14 MeV results in a decrease in elastic scattering but also an increase in inelastic 93

scattering which, overall, increases the damage cross section. 94

Crucially, however, by crossing inelastic channel thresholds, the nature of the PKA’s action after being 95

displaced is altered. The fission reactor (BR2) delivers a broad spectrum with 〈ܧ〉≈1 −2 MeV in which 96

damage is dominated by elastic and low-lying (n,n′) events that generate compact, near-threshold 97

cascades. Visually, this appears in cross-section HRTEM as patchy fringe washout and local c-axis kinks; 98

quantitatively, our iFFT analysis yields a clear rise in in-plane damage metrics across BR2-LD/HD, while c- 99

axis changes are modest once sampling is large. By contrast, the bimodal internal neutron field produced 100

by the 14 MeV irradiation produces both a BR2-like elastic signature from the 1–3 MeV secondaries 101

(though weaker due to lower fluence), and vacancy-rich, branched subcascades from the 10–13 MeV 102

inelastic secondaries. Together with the pure 14 MeV neutrons, the forward-scattering “null” is lifted and 103

momentum transfer is increased, driving the resulting vacancy supersaturation in an oxygen-sensitive 104

lattice that disrupts in-plane registry in the CuO₂ sheets. Here we emphasize that the 14 MeV case had 105

several damage-metric medians comparable to the BR2 samples, despite being irradiated 4-5 orders of 106

magnitude less. In other words, the individual energies of the impinging neutrons seemed to outweigh 107

their collective magnitude when it came to the degree of the damage—specifically the in-plane 108

registry/mosaicity (shear, kinks) of the Cu–O network. 109

As for the lack of large isolated amorphous clusters, it could be that the 14 MeV spectrum produces 110

more events above the “subcascade threshold” (20–40 keV PKAs in complex oxides [28]) that result in the 111

primary recoil fragmenting into multiple subcascades rather than one compact thermal spike. In other 112

words, the energy is distributed over several smaller lobes rather than one big molten core, as 113

corroborated by the many faint, distributed defect clusters seen in the 88-Inch sample TEM—as opposed 114

to the globular ~20 nm clusters of the fission samples. Since the high-dose fission set was irradiated to 115

such higher fluences, it may well be that the exceedingly rare large amorphous clusters found were the 116

result of sporadic coalescence events involving the elastic-scatter-induced compact cascade signatures. 117

The fusion-like case by contrast instead resulted in fewer compact spikes and more spread-out 118


<!-- Page 21 -->


subcascades, so combined with the lower fluence, overlaps into singular, 20-nm features were likely 119

improbable—or at least rare enough to avoid direct observation via TEM. 120

With regards to the void/cavity formation and alignment, under the 14 MeV field, the higher steady- 121

state vacancy excess and radiation-enhanced diffusion enable intragranular cavitation (equiaxed, 122

sometimes faceted voids) and sink-biased cavitation along c-parallel line/planar sinks (BZO rods, threading 123

defects, vertical GB segments, etc.). The same forward-biased PKA vectors that set the subcascade 124

anisotropy also favor co-linear vacancy inflow into c-aligned sinks, giving the track-like cavities seen only 125

in the 14 MeV samples. Beam heating may have also partially accelerated surface diffusion and faceting 126

of pre-existing cavities. This cavitation interpretation is consistent with the quantitative straightness 127

metrics and with the absence of gas-bubble signatures (i.e. lack of HAADF/BF contrast pressure halos, 128

etc.). The thermal peak common to fission reactor spectra would have resulted in tremendous (n,γ) 129

reactions that can recoil REBCO atoms off its host sites, however we see that they anneal efficiently 130

enough to preclude such cavitation effects in the BR2 sample. Unterrainer et al. showed the deleterious 131

effect of thermal neutrons [9] (especially on rare earths like gadolinium with enormous thermal-neutron 132

cross sections), but given that they are not expected in significant fluences at the compact fusion reactor’s 133

magnet location [5], most recent irradiation experiments on REBCO account for this discrepancy by 134

shielding samples in cadmium foil. Overall, however, we contend that, even if thermal neutrons are 135

shielded against, fast fission neutrons fall short of emulating the ~14 MeV neutronicity, secondary light 136

particles, and long but less dense/localized damage tracks expected from DT fusion neutrons. 137

Moreover, the question at the intersection of nuclear physics and superconducting condensed matter 138

physics remains: how would 14 MeV neutron irradiation affect the superconducting properties of REBCO? 139

Unfortunately, at the time of writing, LBNL’s Berkeley Center for Magnet Technology (BCMT) did not have 140

the controls in place to perform high-fidelity transport measurements on radioactive superconductors like 141

our 88-Inch Cyclotron irradiated samples—again speaking to the uniqueness of this cross-lab 142

collaboration. We may, however, link the performance changes noted in the previous transport 143 measurement study of these BR2 samples to our observed microstructural changes and thus make 144 informed inferences about how the properties of the 88-Inch samples may have changed. For example, 145

with respect to the BR2 samples and based on our iFFT results, we expect an altered critical current 146

(enhanced or reduced based on whether the irradiation-induced APC density is past the critical pinning 147

density) as well as a mostly preserved in-plane phase stiffness and Tc (at least relative to the 88-Inch 148

samples). 149

The results in the former study by Iio et al. showed that the SCS-BR2-LD sample experienced a ~10 K 150

decrease in its transition temperature Tc (from about 90 K pristine to 80 K at 8.23×1021 n/m2) and a field- 151

dependent (complex) and temperature-dependent (linear) decrease in normalized critical current, Ic/Ic0. 152

Regarding field-dependence, we see for example in the ܤ∥ܿ configuration at 50 K, that Ic/Ic0 was ~32% 153

at 5 T, ~22% at 10 T, and ~14% at 15 T—a reasonably linear degradation—yet at ܤ∥ܿ, 20 K, Ic/Ic0 was 154

~61% at 5 T, and ~63% for 15 T and 10 T, a reversal of this trend. This implies so-called atomic-scale weak 155

pins probably account for a large portion of the total pins present since, unlike large-scale strong pins, 156

they lack resilience against thermally-activated flux creep at higher temperatures. This is corroborated by 157

the BR2 TEM data which shows no apparent saturation of visible large amorphous clusters on samples 158

with nonzero Jc, which strongly implies that the irradiation-induced pins are largely invisible to TEM—as 159

would be the case for 0D weak pins. Moreover, since  Ic/Ic0 < 1.0 regardless of test condition, we may 160

also conclude that whatever the mix of strong and weak pins, their collective concentration, induced by 161

the 8.23×1021 n/m2 fluence, was past the optimal density. Regarding the temperature-dependence, it was 162


<!-- Page 22 -->


found for example that in the ܤ∥ܿ configuration at 0 T, that Ic/Ic0 was ~60% at 20 K, ~40% at 40 K, and 163

2% at 77 K—a linear degradation. It was pointed out that their unshielded samples saw consistent Tc 164

degradation rates to the unshielded samples in the landmark work by Fischer et al. [15], and discuss the 165

immense contribution of thermal neutrons to this. Defects to ideal copper-oxide plane and chain 166

structures act as scattering centers for the Cooper pairs in d-wave superconductors like REBCO, and since 167

these are introduced linearly as a function of fluence, we expect a linear decline in the critical 168

temperature—exactly what is observed. Our computational analysis that revealed pronounced c-axis 169

bending but only modest mosaic broadening does predict localized strain/kinks that meander the lattice 170

out of plane but does not imply widely disrupted in-plane registry of the CuO2 network. In other words, 171

for the critical temperature, our model does predict the degradation, but it undersells the effects because 172

it is largely agnostic to the oxygen defect signature. 173

This does not bode well for the 14 MeV case. Simultaneous increases in both mosaicity and curvature 174

in both projections, in addition to the now open oxygen-involved channels, imply wider-area 175

misorientation of CuO2 planes plus interlayer shear and oxygen off-stoichiometry—all of which are more 176

pair-breaking than the fission-neutron-induced pattern. After all, the forerunning study but Iio et al. 177

showed that the SCS-BR2-HD samples had completely suppressed superconductivity, yet the 88-Inch 178

microstructure, exposed to substantially lower fluences, had almost equivalent damage metrics. Simply 179

put, pure 14 MeV neutron irradiation—so far very scarcely reported in the literature for 2g HTS REBCO 180

coated conductors—stands to result in the largest Tc suppression rate on record. However, not all is lost: 181

the 14 MeV neutrons generated distributed subcascades that should increase the global pinning force 182

faster than the fission case, beneficial as long as the critical fluence is not reached during the reactor 183

lifetime. Furthermore, even though the large voids—like the large amorphous clusters—are substantially 184

bigger than the ideal ~1-3 nm diameter per fluxon, they may be suitable to act as strong, temperature- 185

resistant pinning centers for flux bundles. Ultimately, however, in order to ascertain the precise critical 186

pinning/current density of this relatively unexplored defect signature, more sophisticated measurements 187

are required. 188

In particular, we stress the need for characterization in as representative environments as possible, i.e., 189

under cryogenic, high-field, representative-flux conditions—often referred to as in-situ. Analog in-situ ion 190

studies revealed modified behavior compared to experiments that involved characterization after 191

significant time periods had passed post-irradiation (i.e. ex-situ), likely due to slow ambient-temperature 192

annealing. Sorbom for example found that the irradiation temperature irrevocably carries consequences 193

on critical current  [12]. Iliffe et al. built on Sorbom’s cryogenic but ex-situ run and showed that the 194

normalized critical current decline in-situ as a function of dose was almost the same as ex-situ—but the 195

in-situ samples saw a recovery of critical current after an extended room temperature anneal [29]. 196

Building on their theory that irradiation induces permanent displacement of oxygen outside of the REBCO 197 layer, it could be that colder temperatures mitigate this release while warmer temperatures promote it. 198 In this way, both cold and warm samples would experience deviations in pristine oxygen content, but 199 more oxygen atoms of the cold sample would remain inside the superconducting layer in interstitial sites. 200 This means that the extended room temperature anneal would allow the cold sample’s oxygens to diffuse 201 back to their proper lattice position within the unit cell, a process which would be greatly reduced for the 202 warmer ex-situ samples with their lack of oxygen atoms altogether. Under this hypothesis, irradiating 203 REBCO with 14 MeV neutrons cold could result in a higher retention of oxygens, alleviating to some extent 204 the anticipated 14 MeV-enhanced decline predicted by this study. This is not certain, nor is the nature of 205 the critical current and irreversibility field modifications due to fusion-spectra alterations of the pinning 206


<!-- Page 23 -->


landscape. In short, we cannot overstate how crucial follow-on in-situ 14 MeV neutron irradiation 207 studies—designed to specifically assess the critical parameters under relevant neutron fluxes, at 208

temperature, and at field—are to the commercial success of near-term compact fusion. 209

Methods 211

Two distinct sets of REBCO-coated conductor samples were investigated in this study. The first set was 212

irradiated in the Belgian Reactor 2 (BR2), a high-flux thermal reactor, while the second set was irradiated 213

at the 88-Inch Cyclotron at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, which provided the harder, fusion- 214

like neutron spectrum. The BR2 sample set included conductors fabricated by two commercial 215

manufacturers, SuperPower® and Fujikura Ltd, to evaluate the role of fabrication method and thin-film 216

chemistry on radiation-induced response. The 88-Inch sample set included only SuperPower® tapes, but 217

consisted of several different models. An overview of BR2 irradiations can be found in [30], and an 218

overview of the 88-Inch Cyclotron irradiation procedure as well as details of both sample sets and specific 219

irradiation conditions are summarized in Table 1. 220

Belgian Reactor 2 samples. Both manufacturers utilized ion beam-assisted deposition (IBAD) of 221

biaxially-textured MgO on Hastelloy C-276 substrates. SuperPower® tapes employed Metal-Organic 222

Chemical Vapor Deposition (MOCVD) to form the REBCO layer, while Fujikura utilized Pulsed Laser 223

Deposition (PLD). SuperPower’s Surround Copper Stabilizer with Advanced Pinning (SCS4050-AP) was 224

examined, which features a 50 µm substrate and multi-rare-earth-based REBCO with BZO nanorods for 225

flux pinning. These were compared to Fujikura’s Copper Stabilized (FYSC-SCH04) tapes, which feature a 226

75 µm substrate and yttrium-based REBCO with BHO pinning. The SuperPower® and Fujikura Ltd. tapes 227

were cut into 32 mm × 4 mm × 0.1 mm strips for irradiation, with one-millimeter-wide segments of these 228

strips cut for post-irradiation spectroscopy measurements. On average, SuperPower® samples were 0.914 229

g and Fujikura samples were 1.257 g, as inferred from geometry and material composition. 230

Unshielded REBCO-coated conductor samples were irradiated at the Belgian Reactor 2 (BR2) to a lower- 231

dose (“LD” in-text) fast-neutron fluence of 8.23×1021 n/m2 and a higher-dose (“HD”, leaving “P” for 232

pristine) fast-neutron fluence of 7.92×1022 n/m2 using low-flux BAM1 capsules in the absence of a Cd 233

shield, at temperatures between 80–100 ℃. Activity was measured with an ORTEC (SEIKO EG&G) high- 234

purity germanium detector (15 cm standoff, 1.8 keV resolution at 1.33 MeV) 1083 days (almost exactly 3 235

calendar years) after irradiation, enabling dose rate estimation post-irradiation. These samples remained 236

highly radioactive at the time of handling (3.06 mCi for SuperPower, and 4.28 mCi for Fujikura some 6.5 237

yr post-irradiation) and required various levels of containment, as shown in Fig. 9a and Fig. 9b. For clarity, 238

we will use the aforementioned labelling convention, in which, say, a SuperPower tape irradiated in the 239

BR2 to the lower dose will be referred to as “SCS-BR2-LD” for example. 240

88-Inch Cyclotron samples. In addition to the BR2 samples, a sample set composed of 35 REBCO strips 241

was irradiated at the 88-Inch Cyclotron at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. In this irradiation, only 242

SuperPower tapes were used, though several varieties: SCS2030-AP, SCS2030-HM, and SCS4030-AP. 243

Again, 32× 0.1 mm snippets were used, with 2- and 4-mm widths depending on the variety. These samples 244

were adhered to an aluminum holder (or “cassette”) with Kapton tape as shown in Fig. 9c, before being 245

placed at the end of the beamline as shown in Fig. 9d and Fig. 9e. The irradiation procedure used was 246

developed by Morrell et al., who used a combined five-parameter model that describes the double- 247

differential TTDB neutron production cross section to replicate deuterium-tritium fusion neutrons [31]. In 248

essence, the neutron beam has a spectral variation as a function of angle—effectively a neutron field— 249


<!-- Page 24 -->


with an intensity carrying units of neutrons per microcoulomb per megaelectronvolt per steradian 250

(n/µC/MeV/Sr). As evidenced with the dark patch in the radiochromic film after beam tuning in Fig. 9f, 251

and visualized in Fig. 9g, this means that while the central “cone” had 14 MeV neutrons, as one moves 252

away from the central angle, the energy and flux decreases according to the double differential described 253

in Morrell’s work. While this spatial variation makes giving an exact fluence analogous to the BR2 samples 254

difficult, we can say with confidence that the central beam spot flux was ~1 × 1016 n/m2/s. Since these 255

samples were exposed to the field for 6 seconds in the case of cassette 1 (“C1”) and 60 seconds for 256

cassette 2 (“C2”), we find the respective fluences C1 ≅6 × 1016 n/m2 and C2 ≅6 × 1017 n/m2. While 257

tracking temperature was not possible we may estimate from first principles that the neutron beam 258

heating was on the order of mW. Although minor activation occurred (~0.25 mrem/h on contact, ~0.03 259

mrem/hr at 30 cm), the samples were deemed suitable for direct handling under “As low as reasonably 260

achievable” or ALARA-guided protocols during preparation and imaging. By our labelling convention, the 261

lower dose samples used for activation analysis were “SCS-88-Inch-C1” and the higher dose for 262

microscopy “SCS-88-Inch-C2”. A single ORTEC GMX Series (model GMX-50220-S) High-Purity Germanium 263 (HPGe) detector was used to assay the 88-Inch samples. This detector is a nitrogen-cooled coaxial n-type 264 HPGe with a 0.5 mm beryllium window, and a 64.9 mm diameter, 57.8 mm long crystal. 265

Subsample processing and mounting. Since the flux and energies of the neutrons used varied across 266

the length of each strip of tape, small ~5–7 mm subsample cutlets were harvested from each. These were 267

made using a standardized protocol to preserve microstructural integrity and ensure reproducibility 268

across imaging sessions. Cutting was performed during submersion in ethanol using a diagonal-vertical- 269

diagonal sequence to maintain knowledge about each subsample’s chirality. Following segmentation, 270

chemical etching was applied to expose specific functional layers—REBCO, copper, silver, or Hastelloy— 271

depending on the analysis objective (though not reported here, each major layer was additionally 272

Image pre-processing. Images were standardized to 1024×1024 using bicubic interpolation [34] to 365 preserve edge continuity while limiting aliasing. A Gaussian blur (σ = 0.8) was applied prior to binarization, 366 followed by global Otsu thresholding [35], small-object removal, and morphological opening/closing [36] 367 (disk radius = 2) to connect 1–2-px interruptions and smooth edges without materially changing ridge 368 thickness. The medial axis transform [37] produced a 1-px centerline; spurs shorter than 12 px were 369 pruned to limit skeletonization artifacts. Images originally at 512×512 were upscaled to 1024×1024 before 370 segmentation to equalize sampling, which reduces bias in curvature- and spectrum-based metrics. 371 Implementations used OpenCV [38], scikit-image [39], and SciPy [40]. 372

[42] with fixed segment parameters to ensure comparability. The following metrics were used to 378

reading the TEM images with initial resolutions of 1024×1024 or 512×512, they are first standardized to a 423

underwent contrast normalization through Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE) 426

[49], a local histogram-based method that prevents over-amplification of noise by limiting contrast 427

enhancement in uniform regions with hyperparameters clip limit set to 8 and tile grid size set to (16,16). 428

Binary Segmentation and Contour Extraction. We apply Otsu’s thresholding algorithm to contrast- 429

processed grayscale images, which computes an optimal global threshold by minimizing intra-class 430

variance between foreground and background pixel intensities. The resulting binary mask serves as input 431

for contour detection using the Teh-Chin chain approximation algorithm [50] in the Suzuki and Abe border 432

following algorithm [51]. This method encodes continuous contours as a sequence of polygonal segments. 433

Feature Filtering and Angular Dispersion Calculation. We further analyze contours above a tunable area 434

threshold, to exclude noise, using Principal Component Analysis (PCA). For each contour, PCA determines 435

the direction of maximum variance, corresponding to the dominant orientation of the feature, which is 436

encoded in the first eigenvector. We compute the orientation angle using the two-argument arctangent 437

function. To account for crystallographic symmetry in REBCO, we model anisotropy modulo π, thus 438

mapping angular dispersion to the interval [0, π]. For pristine images only, knowing the truth value of the 439

orientation of the images, we exclude angles in the lower 40th percentile from the angular dispersion 440

distributions to remove noise. To focus on meaningful structural features, we filter all distributions with 441

a minimum of 1000 pixels and only resulting contours within the 70th to 97th percentile range of area are 442

retained, as larger contours are associated with physically significant defect aggregates and exhibit 443

stronger eigenvalues in PCA. 444

Sources of Error 496

All computational analysis occurs downstream from sampling and imaging, thus any upstream flaws may 497 lead to analytical errors. Possible sources of error at the sampling level include non-uniform lamella 498 preparation and differences in local thickness. At the imaging level, errors may arise from inconsistent 499 illumination and contrast, repeated tiles from the same region (which risks pseudoreplication), and spatial 500 bias (e.g. over-representation of defect-rich zones in the data). Many processing steps rely on fixed 501 parameter values, such as fixed-radius morphological operations, minimum length cutoffs, and, in 502 particular, mask designs and parameters. We mitigate these sources of error by carefully tuning any 503 parameters to match the data, however poor parameter selection would affect the results. Additionally, 504 while per-image medians reduce sensitivity to outliers and fragmentation they do not eliminate them 505 entirely. Analyses based on 12 and bootstrap confidence intervals assume that images are independent, 506 an assumption which may be violated if many tiles come from a single micrograph or area on a sample. 507 Finally, unequal group sizes can introduce biases when comparing groups. We also note that for the PCA 508 analysis, the code largely identified the atomic fringes as the principal component, analogous to ࢍࢉ iFFT 509 bands but sometimes did identify in-plane registry more analogous to ࢍࢇ࢈ iFFT bands. While this signature 510 does have consequences on the angular dispersion, the effect itself was clearly enhanced for irradiated 511 REBCO micrographs. In other words, the reported angular dispersions do reflect irradiation-induced 512 changes to the REBCO lattice, albeit partially indirectly since the damaged microstructure resulted in a 513 proportionally higher detection of ab-like principal components. 514
